item.title: In Vivo CRISPR Base Editing of ANGPTL3 for Durable Lipid Lowering.
item.abstract: Circulating concentrations of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) and triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are leading risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease1. Despite several approved lipid-lowering medications, most patients fail to achieve target lipid levels under the chronic care treatment model2,3. Here, we describe a potential single-course treatment in which an infusion of guide RNA and mRNA encoding a CRISPR adenine base editor-encapsulated within a GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle-leads to durable, liver-selective inactivation of angiopoietin-like 3 (ANGPTL3), a known driver of increased LDL-C and triglyceride concentrations. Analyses in human liver cells in vitro confirmed that the base editor introduces a DNA base-pair change at the target ANGPTL3 locus with no detectable off-target editing at any of approximately 3000 candidate sites or treatment-related structural variants. Targeted ANGPTL3 inactivation in nonhuman primates was well-tolerated and led to a > 90% mean reduction in circulating ANGPTL3 protein, with durability confirmed out to 3 years following a single dose. In mouse and nonhuman primate models of hyperlipidemia, gene inactivation was associated with reductions of approximately 40 to 50% in LDL-C and 50 to 70% in triglycerides. These results provided the scientific foundation for initiation of an ongoing first-in-human clinical trial in patients with refractory hyperlipidemia syndromes.

item.title: Development of mitochondrial base editing technology and its application in animals.
item.abstract: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations constitute major genetic determinants of mitochondrial disorders and contribute to the progressive dysfunction of energy-demanding tissues. However, precise manipulation of the mitochondrial genome remains a formidable challenge for decades due to the unique structural and biological features of mitochondria. Recent breakthroughs in mitochondrial base-editing technologies address longstanding barriers in mitochondrial genome engineering by enabling programmable nucleotide conversion without introducing DNA double-strand breaks. Mitochondrial base editing evolves rapidly from a proof-of-concept strategy in cultured cells into a versatile platform for generating animal models, dissecting mitochondrial gene function and exploring therapeutic interventions for mitochondrial diseases. Recent advances enable the creation of animals carrying defined pathogenic mtDNA variants and provide initial evidence supporting the feasibility of in vivo mitochondrial genome correction and disease amelioration. Here, we review the evolution of mitochondrial base-editing technologies and summarize the major editing platforms, with particular emphasis on recent advances in editor engineering, expansion of targeting capabilities, generation of animal disease models and emerging therapeutic applications. We further discuss the remaining challenges, including editing precision, target-site accessibility, delivery efficiency, and comprehensive safety evaluation. Finally, we highlight future opportunities for developing next-generation mitochondrial genome-editing systems and advancing their translation toward clinical applications.

item.title: From prediction to creation: How AI-driven design is reshaping microbial biocatalysis.
item.abstract: Enzyme engineering has long relied on rational design and directed evolution, yet both remain bounded by natural enzyme space - a constraint felt acutely across the largely uncharacterised microbial world. The 2021 advent of accurate structure prediction marked an inflection point, catalysing AI methods that now extend far beyond folding. These tools are organism-agnostic; the microbial domain is their proving ground because it supplies both the uncharacterised sequence space and the expression hosts. Here we examine three stages: mining microbial sequence space; generative design, whether conditioned on structure or sequence; and machine learning-guided directed evolution. We trace the trajectory from reading the protein universe toward writing it, asking where each has delivered for microbial biocatalysis. Because published claims are hard to compare, we propose a tiered framework - catalysis, selectivity, producibility, process fit - for judging whether an AI-designed enzyme is a useful biocatalyst rather than merely a functional protein.

item.title: Spatial control of enzyme orientation at the lipid droplet interface enables regio- and chemoselective metabolic flux.
item.abstract: Precise spatial control over multienzyme cascade reactions is increasingly recognized as a design lever in synthetic biology for enhancing catalytic performance and directing metabolic flux. By emulating principles of cellular compartmentalization, synthetic scaffolds and engineered interfaces have emerged as powerful platforms to modulate intermediate channeling and reaction efficiency in complex biocatalytic systems. However, robust and spatially defined immobilization of multienzyme assemblies within physicochemically optimal compartments remains challenging because of the dynamic intracellular environment. Here, we reprogram the amphiphilic interface of yeast lipid droplets (LDs) as a programmable scaffold system to support regio- and chemoselective localization of enzymes. Guided by molecular dynamics simulations, we designed LD-anchoring motifs to direct the enzyme orientation at the LD monolayer interface, yielding cytosol-facing or LD inner-facing configurations. Using this designed LD-anchoring motif, we spatially reorganize a trienzyme cascade for prodeoxyviolacein (PDV) biosynthesis across the cytosol-LD interface, facilitating directional conversion of hydrophilic substrates into hydrophobic products. This spatial reorganization substantially improved PDV production by 1300%, achieving 46.25 milligrams per liter. Our approach offers a modular and tunable platform for engineering spatially organized and readily deployable enzyme cascades, opening avenues for biosynthetic catalysis at organellar interfaces.

item.title: Phyfold: environment aware mathematical modeling for protein folding dynamics integrated with physics informed neural network.
item.abstract: Protein folding remains a fundamental problem in computational biology, where understanding folding trajectories and dynamic behavior under physiological conditions is critical for linking structure to function. Recent advances such as AlphaFold have revolutionized sequence to structure prediction, establishing a powerful and robust foundation for computational protein modeling. Building upon this success, we introduce a novel physics informed computational framework that expands static structure prediction toward dynamic and physically consistent modeling of protein folding processes. The proposed framework unifies a mathematically grounded reaction diffusion model of folding kinetics with deep sequence embeddings through a physics informed neural network (PINN), ensuring consistency with governing physical laws while remaining biologically grounded. We refer to this unified framework as PhyFold. Our results illustrate that the proposed approach effectively captures environment dependent folding dynamics and shows strong agreement with both numerical reference solutions and experimental fluorescence measurements under physiologically relevant conditions. By explicitly integrating environmental factors such as temperature, pressure, and pH, PhyFold enables realistic, physics aware simulation of protein folding dynamics. This approach offers a natural extension of modern structure prediction methods and opens new directions for protein design, structure guided drug discovery, and personalized medicine. The code to reproduce the work is available at https://github.com/jamshaidwarraich/PhyFold.git .Scientific contributionPhyFold introduces a hybrid Bio-Physics Informed Neural Network framework that models protein folding kinetics as a reaction diffusion partial differential equation with environmentally modulated kinetic coefficients, integrated with ProtT5 sequence embeddings for sequence specific spatiotemporal prediction an approach not previously demonstrated in the literature. Unlike purely data driven or static structure prediction methods, PhyFold explicitly encodes temperature, pH, and pressure dependence into governing kinetic coefficients, enabling physically interpretable simulation of cooperative folding transitions across diverse physiological conditions. Dual validation against finite difference reference solutions and experimental GFP fluorescence measurements confirms mathematical consistency and biological relevance, establishing PhyFold as a computationally efficient surrogate for environment aware protein folding dynamics.

item.title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters.
item.abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.
item.authors: A Barghout, Chiñas Serrano, Sanchez-Lengeling, et al.

item.title: Vorinostat Can Reduce an Ongoing Fibrosis and Preserve Key Liver Metabolic Functions by Selectively Altering Mesenchymal Cell Differentiation
item.abstract: Liver fibrosis is a major global cause of mortality that is driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing myofibroblasts (MyoFs). The lack of predictive human in vitro models has severely hampered the discovery of targeted anti-fibrotic therapies. Here, we describe a human iPSC-derived hepatic micro-organoid (microHO) model, which labels collagen producing cells, to study liver fibrosis pathophysiology and screen drug candidates. We discovered that while multiple drugs prevented fibrosis when co-administered prophylactically with TGF{beta}1, only the FDA-approved pan-HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat (SAHA) successfully reduced an established, ongoing fibrosis and preserved life-sustaining liver metabolic functions in a fibrotic microenvironment, including ammonia detoxification and CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism. To uncover its mechanism of action, we utilized single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR-Cas12a lineage tracing. We found that Vorinostat actively redirects HSC differentiation away from pro-fibrotic MyoFs and toward a distinct, fibrosis-suppressing mesenchymal inhibitory (MesInh) cell. By reversing TGF{beta}1-induced epigenetic silencing, Vorinostat opens condensed chromatin to rescue metabolic gene expression and generates anti-fibrotic effectors that neutralize ongoing TGF{beta}1 signaling. Given its distinct capacity to remodel mesenchymal cell fate and reverse epigenetic repression of metabolic genes at clinically achievable concentrations, Vorinostat represents a highly promising drug for repurposing as a therapeutic for advanced human liver fibrosis.

item.title: Dual-targeted bioengineered bacterial extracellular vesicles ameliorate senile osteoporosis via SAE1-mediated NAT10 SUMOylation and ac4C-dependent glycolysis.
item.abstract: Senile osteoporosis (SOP) is an age-related skeletal disease characterized by progressive bone loss and the deterioration of bone microarchitecture. Promoting the osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) is a potential strategy for SOP intervention; however, achieving targeted regulation of BMSCs with translational feasibility remains challenging. Given the modifiability, biocompatibility, and production potential of bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs), this study constructed dual-targeted bioengineered BEVs (BT-BEVs-CS) via synthetic biology. These BT-BEVs-CS display the bone-targeting peptide Ser-Asp-Ser-Ser-Asp (SDSSD, BT), the chemokine receptor CXCR4, and SUMOylation activating enzyme subunit 1 (SAE1) to promote the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs. In vitro and in vivo experiments showed that, via the synergistic action of CXCR4 and BT, BT-BEVs-CS targeted the bone microenvironment and were internalized by BMSCs. Mechanistic studies suggested that targeted delivery of SAE1 promoted the SUMOylation of N-acetyltransferase 10 (NAT10), thereby attenuating its ubiquitin-mediated degradation. Stabilized NAT10 subsequently supported the N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification of the mRNA encoding phosphoglucose isomerase (PGI), enhancing PGI mRNA stability. This modification contributed to increased PGI expression, enhanced glycolytic activity, and improved energy support for the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs. In vivo studies further showed that BT-BEVs-CS facilitated the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs and ameliorated pathological bone loss in SOP mouse models. In summary, this study constructed bioengineered BT-BEVs-CS with bone-targeting and osteoinductive properties. This work provides insights into the mechanisms of the SAE1-NAT10/ac4C-PGI regulatory axis in post-translational modifications (PTMs), RNA epigenetic regulation, and glycolysis, offering a preclinical proof-of-concept for targeted nano-intervention strategies for SOP.

item.title: Mesenchymal Stromal Cell-Derived Secretome for Diabetic Foot Ulcers: Therapeutic Potential, Challenges in Clinical Translation, and Future Directions.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) represent one of the most challenging chronic complications of diabetes mellitus, developing in approximately 15 to 25% of affected individuals over their lifetime and imposing a substantial burden on healthcare systems worldwide. Even with coordinated, multidisciplinary wound management strategies, a substantial proportion of these ulcers fail to heal in a timely manner, predisposing patients to secondary infection, lower-limb amputation, and elevated mortality risk. Mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) have long been investigated as a regenerative treatment option given their reparative capacity; however, translating live-cell therapy into routine practice has been hindered by limited post-transplantation cell viability, inefficient tissue engraftment, and the practical difficulties of large-scale cell manufacturing. As an alternative, attention has shifted toward the MSC-derived secretome a complex mixture of extracellular vesicles, cytokines, chemokines, trophic factors, and microRNAs which appears to preserve much of the parent cells regenerative and immune-modulating activity without the drawbacks associated with administering live cells.
METHODS: In this review, we examine the biological composition and mechanistic actions of the MSC secretome as they relate to DFU repair, focusing specifically on strategies for topical application.
RESULTS: Evidence from preclinical diabetic wound models points to accelerated wound closure, stimulation of new blood vessel formation, remodeling of the extracellular matrix, and dampening of persistent inflammatory activity following secretome treatment. Findings from early clinical trials have likewise been encouraging, with rates of complete wound closure ranging from 62 to 100% across two limited studies enrolling between 10 and 110 participants, with outcomes varying according to the cellular origin of the secretome, the route by which it was delivered, and differences in study design. Several barriers still limit clinical adoption. GMP-compliant production protocols have not been harmonized across manufacturers. Batches vary from one production run to the next. No validated assay yet exists to measure biological potency. Long-term safety data remain limited, and questions about the appropriate dose are still unresolved. Looking ahead, engineered or modified secretome formulations, combination therapies, and smart wound-monitoring devices may help improve outcomes further.
CONCLUSION: Current evidence supports the MSC secretome as a promising, cell-free option for DFU management. Its place in standard clinical care will depend on large, multicenter randomized controlled trials and on establishing consistent, standardized manufacturing practices.

item.title: ATM promotes nucleolytic processing of reversed replication forks during DNA interstrand cross-link repair.
item.abstract: During replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) repair, fork reversal is thought to enable the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway to resolve the ICL through nucleolytic incisions. The resulting regressed arm of the reversed fork undergoes extensive nucleolytic resection that may facilitate completion of replication. Despite the importance of these remodeling events, their regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we use cell-free Xenopus egg extracts and human cells to investigate reversed fork processing during ICL repair by the FA pathway. We find that the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase is activated concomitantly with fork reversal and promotes resection of reversed fork intermediates. ATM enhances chromatin recruitment of DNA2, which acts alongside EXO1 to resect reversed forks formed during ICL repair. Moreover, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) leads to ATM hyperactivation, accelerated reversed fork processing, and accumulation of aberrant end-joining products, implying that PP2A restrains ATM signaling to limit reversed fork resection. Taken together, this work identifies reversed forks as substrates for ATM activation and reveals a phospho-regulatory circuit that controls reversed fork processing.

item.title: Green synthesis of MgO-Se nanomaterials using Streptomyces and their anti-inflammatory effects in osteoarthritis-like cell models.
item.abstract: Osteoarthritis is associated with persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, and progressive degradation of the cartilage extracellular matrix. This study prepared magnesium oxide nanoparticles (MgO NPs), selenium nanoparticles (Se NPs), and a combined MgO-Se nanomaterial by extracellular biosynthesis using cell-free Streptomyces culture supernatant and evaluated their physicochemical and biological properties. The materials were characterized by ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, field-emission scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and selected-area electron diffraction. The MgO-Se preparation contained coexisting MgO- and Se-associated crystalline phases, exhibited an Mg:Se atomic ratio of approximately 1:2.7, and had a mean particle diameter of 67.22 ± 11.9 nm. At an equal nominal dry-material concentration of 2 μg/mL, MgO-Se maintained cellular compatibility and produced the broadest overall biological response among the tested formulations. In lipopolysaccharide-stimulated RAW264.7 macrophages, MgO-Se reduced nitric oxide, tumor necrosis factor-α, prostaglandin E2, and intracellular reactive oxygen species by 48.96%, 83.80%, 84.30%, and 51.77%, respectively, while shifting polarization-associated gene expression toward a less inflammatory profile. In interleukin-1β-stimulated SW1353 cells, MgO-Se reduced the corresponding mediators by 47.75%, 84.73%, 84.25%, and 71.56%, respectively. It also partially recovered aggrecan and type II collagen expression and suppressed a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs 5 and matrix metalloproteinase-13. item.title: Circulating blood microbiome biomarkers as liquid biopsy in breast cancer.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Circulating tumor material can already be used to help in cancer management, but host-microbiota interactions may add complementary value. This study evaluated a "liquid microbiopsy", combining cell-free microbial DNA (cf-mbDNA) with host biomarkers of microbial translocation/permeability (LBP, sCD14, I-FABP), to refine staging and prognosis in breast cancer.
METHODS: We analyzed 136 individuals: 58 metastatic breast cancer (MBC), 58 early breast cancer (EBC), and 20 healthy donors. Plasma cf-mbDNA was quantified by 16S rRNA qPCR with extraction/run negative controls; LBP, sCD14, I-FABP by ELISA; and CRP by immunoturbidimetry. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) and PD-L1 on CTCs were assessed by CellSearch® and immunostaining. Diagnostic performance was assessed by area under the ROC curve. In MBC, progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and Cox models.
RESULTS: LBP discriminated EBC from MBC with an AUC 0.92, with a slight improvement in the 3- or 5-marker models (AUC 0.936-0.939). For EBC vs healthy donors, CRP showed modest performance (AUC 0.73), and marker combinations offered no improvement.. In MBC (median follow-up 77.5 months), median PFS and OS were 4.5 and 14.5 months, respectively. In univariate analysis, shorter PFS was associated with tumor subtype, > 3 prior treatments, > 2 metastatic sites, CTCs ≥ 5, and PD-L1-positive CTCs detection. In multivariate analysis, sCD14 and I-FABP independently predicted PFS, while sCD14 was independently associated with OS.
CONCLUSIONS: A measurable host-microbiota-barrier axis (LBP, sCD14, I-FABP) provided stage-related and prognostic information complementary to CTC/PD-L1 status, whereas cf-mbDNA load alone showed limited discriminative value. These findings support liquid microbiopsy as a complementary extension of liquid biopsy but must be considered as exploratory, and warrant multicenter validation in larger independent cohorts with standardized pre-analytics and low-biomass controls.

item.title: Microenvironment of Bone and Joint Infection: Examining the Microenvironment.
item.abstract: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is a major complication of arthroplasty, and conventional diagnostic methods for PJI remain limited by suboptimal sensitivity, long turnaround times, high cost, and patient inconvenience, particularly in biofilm-associated and culture-negative infections. Emerging data suggest that the infected joint microenvironment contains host- and pathogen-derived molecular signatures with substantial diagnostic potential. This review evaluates current evidence on microenvironment-related biomarkers in PJI, including host extracellular vesicles, host cell-free nucleic acids (microRNA/cell-free DNA), non-host-derived biomarkers, and sequencing-based pathogen detection techniques. Host-derived biomarkers show favorable discriminatory capability by characterizing inflammatory and immune responses, and metagenomic and sequencing-based technologies improve pathogen identification. Despite encouraging diagnostic performance, widespread clinical implementation remains limited due to a lack of standardization, cost, and limited prospective validation. Future prospective multicenter studies should integrate conventional microbiological methods with molecular and microenvironment-based approaches to improve diagnostic accuracy.

item.title: Borrelia-specific cell-free DNA in plasma from adults with Lyme neuroborreliosis: an explorative study.
item.abstract: Current blood-based diagnostic modalities for LNB have significant limitations. Using Next Generation Sequencing, we investigated blood samples from patients with LNB and non-LNB controls for Borrelia burgdorferi-specific cfDNA (Bb-cfDNA). Blood-samples from 61 adults suspected for LNB were analysed with amplification-free Nanopore metagenomic sequencing and detected cfDNA was cross-referenced with human and Bb-genome databases to identify Bb-specific-cfDNA. Bb-cfDNA was detected in 3 of 45 patients with LNB (6.7%) and in none of the 16 controls. Positive samples contained low levels of Borrelia-classified reads. Bb-cfDNA is unlikely to become a relevant blood-based diagnostic test for LNB in immunocompetent adults.

item.title: Exosomes improved oxidative stress and apoptosis in BPA-induced nephrotoxicity in kidney cells through modulation of Nrf2/Keap1 signaling pathway.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bisphenol A (BPA) is an environmental toxicant known to induce nephrotoxicity primarily through oxidative stress-mediated inflammation and apoptosis. Mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes have recently emerged as promising cell-free therapeutic agents with antioxidant and anti-apoptotic properties. This study aimed to investigate the protective effects of bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell-derived exosomes against BPA-induced nephrotoxicity in human proximal tubular epithelial (HK-2) cells, with particular emphasis on the potential involvement of the Nrf2/Keap1 signaling pathway.
METHODS: HK-2 cells were allocated into four groups: control, BPA, exosome (EXO), and BPA + EXO. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay. Intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS), lipid peroxidation, antioxidant parameters, total antioxidant capacity (TAC), glutathione (GSH) levels, and inflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and IL-10) were evaluated using standard biochemical assays. Protein expression levels of Nrf2, Keap1, Bax, and Bcl-2 were determined by Western blot analysis.
RESULTS: BPA exposure significantly reduced cell viability and antioxidant capacity while increasing ROS production, lipid peroxidation, pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and apoptotic signaling. Exosome treatment markedly attenuated oxidative stress, restored antioxidant defenses, improved inflammatory cytokine balance, and reversed BPA-induced alterations in Nrf2/Keap1 signaling and apoptosis-related protein expression.
CONCLUSION: Bone marrow mesenchymal stromal cell-derived exosomes exert protective effects against BPA-induced cytotoxicity in HK-2 cells by alleviating oxidative stress, modulating the Nrf2/Keap1 signaling pathway, and suppressing apoptosis. Although further mechanistic studies are required to establish causality, these findings highlight the therapeutic potential of exosomes as a cell-free strategy for mitigating environmental toxin-associated renal injury.
